```{r setup, include = FALSE}
# Widgets are not evaluated here so the built vignette stays small; run the
# chunks in R to see the charts.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = FALSE)
library(myIO)
```

myDAR maps a site from a phone walk. Each walk produces a point cloud, a DEM,
a GeoPackage with the track, GPS fixes and accuracy figures, and the device
trajectory. myIO reads those files into data frames and plots them.

## Reading a walk

`read_mydar_walk()` reads a walk output directory:

| File | Element | Reader |
|---|---|---|
| `walk.copc.laz` | `points` | `read_mydar_points()` (needs **rlas**) |
| `terrain.tif` | `terrain` | `read_mydar_terrain()` (needs **terra**) |
| `walk.gpkg` | `track`, `track_points`, `gps_fixes`, `pins`, `features`, `accuracy` | `read_mydar_gpkg()` (needs **sf**) |
| `trajectory.csv` | `trajectory` | `read_mydar_trajectory()` |

myIO does not install rlas, terra or sf; the readers ask for them when they
need them.

```{r read, eval = FALSE}
walk <- read_mydar_walk("path/to/walk", max_points = 20000)
walk
```

A cloud has far more points than an SVG chart can draw, so the reader keeps
`max_points` of them (every k-th point in file order, which keeps the relative
density across the walk) and records the full count. The DEM is aggregated
when it has more than `max_cells` cells. By default x and y are shifted to
meters from the south-west corner of the walk (`walk$origin` holds the
shift), so the axes read in walk-scale meters.

The examples below use `mydar_synthetic_walk`, a synthetic walk from the myDAR
test suite that ships with myIO and needs none of the optional packages. Its
raw files are in `system.file("extdata", "mydar-synthetic", package = "myIO")`.

```{r walk, eval = TRUE}
walk <- mydar_synthetic_walk
walk
```

## The views

### Plan view

Points seen from above, one color per LAS class, with the track and any point
features. Crowded areas read darker, so the chart also shows point density.

```{r plan}
mydar_plan_view(walk, profile = list(from = c(0, 4), to = c(11, 3)))
```

### Terrain

The DEM uses the `raster` chart type: a grid of cells drawn as one image,
colored by height and shaded by a hillshade. Hover a cell for its height.

```{r terrain}
mydar_terrain_view(walk, azimuth = 315, altitude = 45)
```

The raster type works for any regular grid: map `x_var`, `y_var` (cell
centers) and `value`, and optionally `shade` (0-1).

```{r raster-generic}
grid <- expand.grid(x = seq(0, 5, by = 0.1), y = seq(0, 3, by = 0.1))
grid$value <- sin(grid$x) * cos(grid$y)
myIO() |>
  addIoLayer(type = "raster", label = "value", data = grid,
             mapping = list(x_var = "x", y_var = "y", value = "value"),
             options = list(palette = "cividis"))
```

### Profile

Points within a corridor along a line, as height against distance along the
line, with the DEM height along the same line. `mydar_profile()` returns the
corridor points as a data frame.

```{r profile}
mydar_profile_view(walk, from = c(0, 4), to = c(11, 3), width = 0.5)
```

```{r profile-table, eval = TRUE}
head(mydar_profile(walk, from = c(0, 4), to = c(11, 3)))
```

### Uncertainty and QA

```{r qa}
mydar_trajectory_view(walk)
mydar_gps_view(walk)
mydar_sigma_view(walk)
mydar_accuracy_view(walk)
```

`sigma_m` is the per-point 1-sigma per axis that the cloud stores. The
accuracy chart puts shape figures (how well distances inside the walk hold)
next to map position (where the walk sits on the map). On this walk the map
position comes from phone GPS, so it is hundreds of times larger than the
shape figures.

## All at once

`mydar_dashboard()` lays out the views on one page. Brush the plan view and
the same points light up on the profile; hover the uncertainty or GPS chart
and the other shows a cursor at the same moment.

```{r dashboard}
mydar_dashboard(walk)
```
